content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.75. I used 53 of the 60 budget.

**What I did:**
1. I trained the learner on three tasks: L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3. Rules L4, S4 and M4 stayed unseen.
2. I tested other tasks several times each, since a single test result varies a lot (standard deviation about 12 examples).
3. For the deciding step I trained L4-S4-M4. It gives the same response as L1-S4-M4 on none of the 256 inputs, but it contains the two rules L1-S4-M4 was missing.

**Results (average examples needed to reach criterion):**

| Task | Rules new to the learner | Before training L4-S4-M4 | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S4-M4 | 2, then 0 | 37 (4 tests) | 14 (10 tests) |
| L4-S2-M2 | 1, then 0 | 26 (3 tests) | 25 (7 tests) |
| Tasks with all rules familiar | 0 | about 21 (9 tests) | – |
| Tasks with 2–3 new rules | 2–3 | about 35 | – |

**Why part-based:** L1-S4-M4 got about 23 examples cheaper after training a task that matches none of its outputs. That drop is large compared with the noise. Reusing stored rules explains it directly. A learner that stores whole tasks and judges similarity by matching outputs should have gained nothing from that training.

**Why not higher confidence:**
- Tasks with one new rule cost about the same as tasks with none (about 22 vs 21). That is not what a part-based learner would be expected to show.
- L4-S2-M2 should also have got cheaper once its last new rule was trained, and it didn't.
- I can't rule out a holistic learner whose similarity measure counts shared rule labels rather than matching outputs. L1-S4-M4 shares two labels with L4-S4-M4, so such a learner would also predict the drop.
